D001-D008_h001.question:
Ever since I was a kid—teachers used to say it in elementary school—I’ve had trouble sitting still and staying focused. I remember getting in trouble for constantly fidgeting, wandering around the classroom, and blurting out answers. It never really went away. Even now, in my 40s, I feel like I’m always “on,” like there’s a motor running inside me. I pace around my classroom between periods and even at home my wife comments that I can’t just sit on the couch and relax.

At work, I struggle to keep things organized—lesson plans, grading, emails. I’ll start grading a stack of papers, get distracted by an email or a random thought, and then forget what I was doing. My mind drifts in the middle of students talking; it’s like my thoughts jump tracks constantly.

I also talk a lot—my colleagues joke that I can turn any quick chat into a long conversation. A few times a year I do get into these “high” moods where I feel extra energetic and sleep less, but even when I’m not in those phases, the distractibility, disorganization, restlessness, and excessive talking are there all the time.
D001-D008_h001.options:
A. Anorexia Nervosa
    B. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Bipolar I Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)

D001-D008_h002.question:

I start one case note, get pulled off by an email or a random thought, and suddenly I’m down a rabbit hole and the note’s still unfinished an hour later. I double-book appointments or forget to call families back because I can’t keep everything straight, even with calendars and apps.

I’m constantly moving—bouncing my leg in meetings, pacing during phone calls. Coworkers joke that I never sit still. I talk a lot in team meetings, sometimes interrupting without meaning to, and then feel embarrassed later.

My mood does swing sometimes—there are days I feel more upbeat, more driven—but even on calm or low days, the distractibility and restlessness are still there. They don’t come and go with my mood; they’re just…always running in the background.

I’ve always been kind of scattered, even as a kid. My teachers used to write on my report cards that I was bright but “doesn’t pay attention to details” and “rushes through work.” That hasn’t really changed. As a principal, I’ll send out emails with typos or missing attachments, or I’ll misread a schedule and double-book something. I start on a new policy or report, get halfway through, and then it just… fizzles. I jump to the next thing and end up with a dozen half-finished tasks on my desk and at home—laundry half-folded, dishes soaking for days.

My staff joke that I never sit down. I’m constantly pacing the halls, popping into classrooms, fidgeting in meetings. It feels like I’m revved up inside all the time. I catch myself cutting people off in conversations—teachers, parents, even my husband—because I get impatient waiting for them to finish, or I’m afraid I’ll lose my thought.

Every so often I’ll have a few days where I feel extra upbeat and talkative, sleep less, take on too many projects. But even when my mood is “normal,” this restlessness and distractibility are always there, every single day.
D001-D008_h023.options:
A. Body Dysmorphic Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Bipolar I Disorder

D001-D008_h024.question:
I’ve always been kind of scattered, even as a kid. My teachers used to write on my report cards that I was bright but careless, missing points on tests because I’d skip lines or misread questions. That’s still happening at work: I’ll send scripts to the producer with obvious typos or missing lines because my eyes just seem to slide over details. I start an outline, then get distracted by an email, then an idea for a different segment, and suddenly the deadline’s here and I haven’t actually finished anything all the way through.

People at the station joke that I can’t sit still. If I’m in a meeting, my leg is bouncing, I’m fidgeting with my pen, getting up to refill coffee. It feels like this internal motor that doesn’t really shut off. I’ll also jump into conversations before others finish their thought, or talk over colleagues when we’re pitching ideas, and then realize I’ve cut them off.

My mood can swing—sometimes I feel really “up” and energetic for a few days, sometimes low—but the distractibility and restlessness are there all the time, not just when my mood shifts. They’ve pretty much been a constant background since elementary school.
D001-D008_h024.options:
A. Body Dysmorphic Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Bipolar I Disorder

D001-D008_h025.question:
I’ve been like this as long as I can remember, even back in elementary school. Teachers always said I was “bright but scattered.” I’d rush through math sheets and miss stupid little things, like adding an extra zero, even when I knew how to do it. That’s kind of how my work is now with the furniture—if I don’t triple-check, I’ll misread a measurement or drill in the wrong place because my mind has already jumped to the next step.

Clients will text me their specs, and I’ll start a project full of energy, then halfway through I’ll realize I skipped a step or left something unfinished in the shop. It’s not that I don’t care; I lose the thread. Instructions, emails, even simple house stuff—laundry, bills—if it’s not right in front of me, it just falls off my radar.

I’m always moving—pacing in the shop, bouncing my leg, starting three tasks at once. Coworkers and my ex used to say I act like I’m “plugged in.” I cut people off a lot without meaning to, jump into conversations, answer before folks finish talking. 

I do have times when my mood goes up or down, but this restless, distracted feeling is there all the time, not just when I’m in a good or bad mood.
D001-D008_h025.options:
A. Body Dysmorphic Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Bipolar I Disorder
